summary: Wayne Hathaway backs Edwin Meyer's opposition in RFC 492 to the fixes proposed in RFC 467, arguing that they hide the real problem of lost messages. He proposes using an unused byte in the message leader as a Sequence Control Byte, a count that lets the receiving NCP spot a lost message.

eli5.summary: Number each letter in a series, so the receiver can tell right away if one went missing.

questions: how to detect lost messages in ncp
subtitle: Wayne Hathaway proposes a Sequence Control Byte in the host message leader so a receiving NCP can spot lost messages at once.

tldr.problem: Messages could be lost between hosts, and fixes proposed in RFC 467 for the lost allocate and half-closed problems tended to mask the real problem of lost messages.
tldr.mechanism: One of the two unused bytes in the level 2 message leader becomes a Sequence Control Byte, a per-link message count. The receiving NCP compares it to the expected value and reports a mismatch with an ERR message.
tldr.outcome: A zero value means no checking, so existing NCPs need not change. The RFC presents the scheme as an interim solution.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 512 as Unknown, and it is not marked as obsoleted or updated. It is an early proposal for the ARPANET host-to-host protocol, offered as an interim measure.

sections.title: Why Lost Messages Matter
sections.content: Wayne Hathaway of AMES-67 seconds Edwin Meyer's strong opposition (in RFC 492) to the proposals in RFC 467 about the lost allocate and half-closed phenomena. He supports Meyer's principles on the half-closed phenomenon and agrees that the lost allocate fix masks the real problem of lost messages. He then proposes an alternative scheme for recognizing lost messages.
sections.eli5: If letters vanish and you only patch the symptoms, you never find out that letters are vanishing. This note goes after the vanishing itself.

sections.title: The Sequence Control Byte
sections.content:
One of the two unused eight-bit bytes in the level 2 message leader would be named the Sequence Control Byte (SCB), essentially a modulo 255 message count kept on each link. The receiving NCP computes the expected SCB from the previous message on the same link and compares.

A discrepancy indicates a lost message, which can be reported immediately with an ERR message (still to be defined) carrying both the received and expected SCBs. That could allow recovery if the sender kept the last several messages for each link. The message with the unexpected SCB should still be processed normally, and the next expected SCB is computed from it.
sections.eli5: Each letter in a stack gets a page number. If the receiver sees page 5 after page 3, it knows page 4 is missing and says so right away.

sections.title: Compatibility and Comparison
sections.content:
An SCB of zero means that no checking is to be done, and the SCB after 255 is 1. Because the level 2 protocol says these two unused bytes must be zero, current NCPs need not change unless checking is wanted. The zero rule also lets RST and ERR messages bypass checking, which avoids possible loops.

The scheme resembles the second scheme in RFC 516 but works per link rather than per host, so it does not require all messages between two hosts to arrive in the order sent, which cannot be guaranteed. Hathaway finds the first RFC 516 scheme weak because an IMP may send a RFNM for a message that never reaches its host, and because saving messages is expensive on swapped systems. He thinks the third scheme, host-to-host acknowledgments, is perhaps the best, but it needs major changes to the level 2 protocol, so an interim solution like this has value.
sections.eli5: A page number of zero means do not check, so old machines that never number their pages keep working just as before.

references.text: RFC 467, the proposals on lost allocate and half-closed that this RFC opposes.
Meyer, E., RFC 492, opposing the RFC 467 proposals.
Postel, J., "Lost Message Detection", RFC 516, May 1973.
